title: 186 repositories rewound overnight
role: You help run the GitHub organization of a big open-source project: more than 1,100 repositories and about 680 developers who can push to them.

source.label: Jenkins project: summary report, git repository disruption incident of Nov 10th (2013)

brief: Sunday, 10 November 2013, early afternoon GMT. Developers write in: the last weeks of work have vanished from the main branches of their plugin repositories. Not one repository: dozens.

steps.situation: A plugin maintainer: "master is two months old. Did someone delete my commits?"
steps.evidence:
$ git fetch origin
 + 9c41e07...2b7f3a1 master     -> origin/master  (forced update)
$ git log --oneline -1 origin/master
2b7f3a1 Release 1.12 (from September)
$ git log --oneline -1 master
9c41e07 Fix NPE in config page

choices.text: Compare the server's branch head with an up-to-date clone, and check the push events
choices.why: `forced update` means the branch pointer was moved back, not that commits were deleted. The newer commits still exist in clones, and usually on the server too.

choices.text: Ask maintainers to re-commit their work from memory
choices.why: The commits aren't gone. Git keeps objects by hash; only the branch names point at old ones.

choices.text: Tell everyone to force-push their local copy right now
choices.why: Some clones are stale too, and repos with several maintainers get a race. Whoever pushes last wins.

steps.situation: It's many repositories, all moved back to commits from about two months ago. What do you do before restoring anything?
steps.evidence:
replication  push git@github.com:example-org/foo-plugin.git  +refs/heads/*:refs/heads/*  ok
replication  push git@github.com:example-org/bar-plugin.git  +refs/heads/*:refs/heads/*  ok
... 184 more

choices.text: Find the common pusher and stop it first, with GitHub support's help and the push logs
choices.why: The cause was found within hours from Gerrit's logs and GitHub support. Restoring while the pusher still runs would be undone again.

choices.text: Start fixing repositories one by one
choices.why: If the source is still pushing, your fixes get rewound. And you don't yet know which repos are hit.

choices.text: Remove push access from all 680 developers
choices.why: It locks out the very people with good clones, and the project's open commit policy is part of its culture.

steps.situation: Cause found: one developer started Gerrit with a half-configured replication plugin. It pointed at a folder of 186 old clones and force-pushed them, its default. How do you restore?

choices.text: Combine three things: up-to-date developers push, GitHub support resets heads, and a script on the events API checks every branch
choices.why: This is what worked. Pushes fixed the popular plugins within a day; the events API script found about a dozen branches support had missed.

choices.text: Leave it all to GitHub support
choices.why: Support restored most heads, but not all. Without your own check, about a dozen branches would have stayed wrong.

choices.text: Force-push whatever clone each admin has
choices.why: An admin's clone can be older than the maintainer's. You'd rewind some branches a second time.

steps.situation: Everything is back by the middle of the next week. What do you change?

choices.text: Record every ref update (who and what) across the org, use per-repository access, ask the host for a no-force-push option
choices.why: The project's own follow-ups. A ref log makes the next rollback a script instead of a week of detective work.

choices.text: Ban force-push and call it solved
choices.why: Helps, but the report notes that a deleted branch does similar damage. You still need a record of ref changes.

choices.text: Name the developer in the report so it doesn't happen again
choices.why: A plugin default and all-or-nothing access made the mistake possible. Blame hides that and teaches people to stay quiet.

debrief.what_happened: Early on 10 November 2013 one of about 680 Jenkins developers started Gerrit with a partly misconfigured replication plugin. It found a local folder with 186 clones of Jenkins repositories, about two months old, and replicated them back to GitHub with a forced push, the plugin's default. Branch heads moved back to old commits; no commits were deleted, only the pointers. Several developers noticed at 12:54 GMT, and the cause was found within hours from Gerrit's logs with GitHub support's help. Developers with current clones pushed them back, which restored the most popular plugins within 24 hours; GitHub support reset most other heads; the team's own script on the GitHub events API found about a dozen branches support had missed. All commits were recovered by the middle of the next week. Follow-ups: continuously record ref updates across the organization, per-repository access control, and a hoped-for option to disable forced pushes. Where you host Git yourself, the report suggests `core.logAllRefUpdates` on the server.
lessons: "Forced update" moves a pointer: the commits are usually still there.
Find and stop the source of a mass change before you restore.
Check the restore with data (push events, SHAs), not with hope.
Protect main branches and log every ref update.
